What a project is

Before we get into schedules and budgets, let's start with the basics. What actually makes something a project? What are the three things you are always trading off against each other? And how do you decide whether a project is even worth doing in the first place? We will walk through all three, and you will get to try each one yourself.

Section 2 of 3

Is it a project, or is it operations?

Here is the easiest way to tell the two apart. A project has a finish line. You start it, you work through it, and one day it is finished and handed over. Replacing a mile of old water main is a project. Operations are the opposite. They never finish. They just keep going, day after day, like treating the water or reading the meters.

The one-question testFramework
Does the work
have a finish line?
→
Yes
No
This is the whole framework, and it really is this simple. One question decides it. Tap a branch to see how it plays out on a real water job.

Why does this matter on day one? Because you run the two in completely different ways. A project needs a plan, a schedule, and a clear finish. Operations need a steady routine. When people treat a project like it is just "a quick job," it tends to drift along with no real finish line and nobody watching the budget.

The fastest way to spot the difference is to look for the end state. If there is a specific thing you are delivering and a date when it is done, handle it as a project. If the work just continues, handle it as operations, with a routine and a budget line.

This shapes how you fund things too. Capital projects compete for money and finish. Operations are the steady baseline cost of service. Mix them together and your capital plan gets muddy and the real cost of both is harder to see.

The three things you are always trading off

Every project balances how much work you take on (scope), how long you have (time), and how much you can spend (cost). You cannot change one without it showing up in the others. If the council adds two blocks to a main job but will not move the deadline or the budget, something gives, and it is usually quality. People call this the iron triangle. Move the corners below and watch it happen.

Turn Scope up a couple of times without adding time or cost. Watch the triangle stretch and the quality dot in the middle turn red. That is the squeeze everyone runs into.

The phases a project moves through

A project officially begins with a charter, the one-page "go ahead." From there it moves through a set of phases called the life cycle. Between the phases are gates, which are simple go or no-go checkpoints. Click a phase to see what happens in it.

The project life cycleProcess · interactive

Plan itScope, schedule, budgetG
Build itDo the workG

Section 3 of 3

Is the project even worth doing?

Before a project gets its charter, someone has to ask the honest question: is this worth the money? The answer is the business case. You do not need to be a finance person to build one. Here is the method.

How to build a business caseMethod
1Add up what it costs to build, up front.
2Add up what it saves or earns each year (fewer main breaks, less lost water, lower energy).
3Turn those future savings into today's dollars and subtract the cost. That gives you the NPV.
4Check two sanity numbers: the payback (how many years to break even) and the benefit-cost ratio (dollars back per dollar spent).

Now run the real numbers on the Millpond main replacement. As you slide, watch two pictures update: a curve showing your money over time, and a bar chart comparing what you spend to what you get back.

Watch the curve. It starts below zero because you spent the money, then climbs as the savings pile up. Where it crosses the middle line, that is your payback. Slide the yearly saving down until the curve never crosses. That is a project that does not pay off.

For a utility that runs on rates, the business case is also a conversation about rates. A positive NPV over the life of the pipe is how you explain to a board, and to the customers paying the bill, why the money is worth spending now. And remember the other side of it. Waiting until the old main finally breaks has its own cost, usually a bigger one.

One more, in your own words

Your crew flushes every fire hydrant every spring. Project or operations, and how would you handle it?
Show the answer
Operations. It happens every year and never finishes, so you handle it with a routine and a line in the budget, not a charter and a schedule. The one-question test settles it: there is no finish line.
What to remember

A project has a finish line. Operations just keep going. You manage the two differently.

Scope, time, and cost are tied together. Change one, and another has to move, or quality pays for it.

A charter starts a project, and the life cycle carries it from kickoff to closeout, with a go or no-go gate between phases.

The business case, made of NPV, payback, and the benefit-cost ratio, tells you whether a project is worth doing before you spend a dollar.
